title: HCF urges reform as health claims spike
full_text:
The chief executive of one of the country's biggest private health insurers says the soaring cost of mental health claims is driving up the price of top-tier gold cover to unsustainable levels, triggering an exodus of people into cheaper plans.
Lorraine Thomas, the chief executive of HCF, which has 2.1 million members, said mental health claims accounted for 90 per cent of the fund's gold-tier claims, with the average benefit paid for overnight private mental health admissions costing more than $15,500.
"What we are finding is the cost of mental health claims puts additional pressure on gold. And without reform, it is really hard to see how it is sustainable for these products to remain affordable," Thomas said in her first interview since being appointed CEO of the not-for-profit giant last year.
The growing strain of mental health on the country's healthcare system is highlighted in a white paper HCF will release on Monday, which warns 1.2 million Australians will downgrade to cheaper health cover unless there is an overhaul of how conditions such as depression, drug and alcohol addiction, and bipolar disorder are treated and funded.
The number of Australians with gold cover has fallen from 40 per cent since 2019 to 28 per cent last year. Over the same period, the average premium for gold cover increased up to 71 per cent. A government consultation paper in July proposed a shake-up of the tiered health insurance model, which many in the industry argue no longer works.
Thomas said hospital admissions for the most serious mental health disorders covered only by gold were costing as much as $23,774 a patient, on par with claims for major surgery such as a knee or hip replacement.
"We are quite concerned. More and more brands are removing gold from sales because of the sustainability challenges, so the costs are not fairly or equally distributed," she said.
The warning comes as Australian private health insurance comes under scrutiny in Canberra, with parliament rejecting Labor's plan to scrap a more generous rebate for people over 65, torpedoing plans to free $3 billion to be spent on new aged care beds.
Insurers say they are open to funding psychiatric care outside the hospital system if allowed because it would prevent more serious hospital admissions, which end up costing funds more. Those services, such as visits to psychiatrists, are not covered by private health insurance.
HCF's white paper, written with input from 40 leaders working in the sector, called for a funding overhaul.
The paper shows the cost of mental health insurance claims across the sector has soared 18 per cent over the past five years. Mental health treatment is mainly limited to those on gold cover.
